This review provides a comparative biomechanical analysis between overhead throwing (baseball pitching) and rotational swinging (the golf swing). Both movements involve rapid proximal-to-distal sequencing across an open kinematic chain, but differ substantially in mechanical constraints, boundary conditions, and control objectives.

## Comparative Mechanics

::: {.callout-note}
## Key Kinematic & Dynamic Contrasts

| Dimension | Baseball Pitching | Golf Swing |
|---|---|---|
| **Kinematic Topology** | Open kinetic chain ending in projectile release | Bilateral closed upper-limb loop acting on elastic shaft |
| **Contact Boundary** | Stride foot landing with active linear braking | Dual ground reaction force centers with rotational couple |
| **Peak Joint Velocities** | Shoulder internal rotation ~7,000 deg/s | Pelvis/torso ~400–800 deg/s; clubhead ~100+ mph |
| **Terminal Constraint** | Ball release (unconstrained post-release dynamics) | Impact collision ($m_{\text{ball}} \approx 45.9\text{ g}$, duration $\approx 450\,\mu\text{s}$) |
:::

## Literature Insights & Primary Sources

### 1. Proximal-to-Distal Kinetic Chain Sequencing
Studies by Feltner &amp; Dapena (1986, 1989) and Hirashima et al. (2002, 2007) demonstrate that distal segment acceleration in throwing is primarily driven by dynamic interaction torques (velocity-dependent Coriolis and cross-coupling terms) generated by the deceleration of proximal segments, rather than distal muscular effort alone.

- **Hirashima et al. (2002):** *"Kinetic chain of overarm throwing."* Demonstrated that angular acceleration of the forearm is heavily induced by shoulder and torso rotation terms.
- **Hirashima et al. (2008):** *"Dynamic contribution of muscular and non-muscular torques during overarm throwing."* Confirmed that interaction torques dominate the final acceleration phase.

### 2. Ground Reaction Force Attribution
Pitching biomechanics literature (Fleisig et al., 1999; MacWilliams et al., 1998) shows that peak lead-leg braking force correlates directly with pelvis angular velocity. In the AffineDrift framework, this matches the moving-base support reaction decomposition where ground reaction forces provide the necessary wrench to arrest linear pelvis momentum and transform it into torso yaw velocity.

## AffineDrift Theoretical Relevance

1. **Passive Coupling Dominance:** Both pitching and golf exhibit a terminal phase where external joint moments are dominated by passive inertial drift ($f(x)$) rather than active muscular control ($G(x)u$).
2. **Transfer Limits:** While interaction force mathematics are universal across multibody formulations, specific joint torque time-histories cannot be transferred between pitching and golf due to differing degree-of-freedom coupling (bilateral hand grip vs. unilateral free arm).
